title: Elevation Outlasts Fire Severity as the Dominant Driver of Post-Fire Vegetation Recovery in Kosciuszko National Park
content: The 2019–2020 Black Summer fires affected approximately 33.5% of Kosciuszko National Park, Australia's largest alpine reserve; post-fire recovery models in Australia have rarely used spatial validation. We quantified recovery across severity classes and elevation zones (2021–2025), tested whether driver importance shifts over time, and whether predictors generalise to unseen locations. A Sentinel-2 Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI)-derived recovery index was modelled with Random Forest at one, three and five years post-fire using twelve predictors and random/spatial cross-validation; SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) importance used bootstrap confidence intervals, and recovery was cross-validated against the Normalized Burn Ratio (NBR). Severity's importance declined sharply (mean |SHAP| 0.116 to 0.019); elevation remained important throughout. Fast-recovery clusters occurred at lower elevation (877 versus 1284 m; P < 0.001), and montane and subalpine trajectories were statistically distinguishable. NDVI overstated recovery relative to NBR every year (P < 0.001). Spatial cross-validation R² stayed near zero regardless of block resolution, versus 0.10–0.16 under random splitting. Fire severity's influence is transient; elevation-mediated differences persist over at least five years, and static covariates cannot predict recovery at unseen sites. Post-fire monitoring should be reassessed periodically rather than prioritised on severity alone; spatial cross-validation should become standard for spatially autocorrelated recovery data.
